title: Shakespeare's Sonnets
author: William Shakespeare
openingText: The collection opens by urging a beautiful young man to marry and have children, so that his beauty will not die with him.
about:
Shakespeare's 154 sonnets were published in 1609, though many were probably written in the 1590s. Each is a fourteen-line poem with a fixed rhyme scheme and a turn in the final couplet. Read in order, they tell a loose, mysterious story.

The first 126 are mostly addressed to a young man of great beauty. The poet urges him to have children, then promises that the poems themselves will make him live forever, and later suffers through jealousy, absence, a rival poet and betrayal. Sonnets 127 to 152 turn to a 'dark lady', a woman the poet desires against his own judgment, in poems that are bitter, funny and frank about sex. Two short poems about Cupid close the collection.

This edition gives each sonnet in Shakespeare's original text next to a plain modern prose version, so you can follow both the meaning and the music. Some of the most famous lines in English are here: 'Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?', 'Let me not to the marriage of true minds', and 'My mistress' eyes are nothing like the sun.'

whyItMatters.title: Love written from the inside
whyItMatters.body: The sonnets track love's whole range: admiration, longing, jealousy, desire, shame and loyalty. They are short enough to read one at a time and still feel personal four hundred years later.

whyItMatters.title: Writing against time
whyItMatters.body: Again and again the poet claims that verse can defeat age and death. Reading the collection lets you judge whether the promise holds.

whyItMatters.title: The craft of fourteen lines
whyItMatters.body: Each sonnet builds an argument and turns it in the last two lines. Comparing the original with the prose version shows how much work the form does.

angleCards.title: The story
angleCards.text: Read the sonnets in order and piece together the relationships between the poet, the young man, the rival poet and the dark lady.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Sonnets as a story and follow the relationships behind them.

angleCards.title: Time and death
angleCards.text: Mark every image of time, age and decay, and how the poet answers it.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the Sonnets' argument about time, beauty and whether poetry can last.

angleCards.title: The couplet
angleCards.text: Read the last two lines of each sonnet first, then the whole poem. How does the turn work?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand how each sonnet's final couplet changes the meaning of the poem.

angleCards.title: Favourites
angleCards.text: Start with 18, 29, 73, 116 and 130, then explore their neighbours.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the most famous sonnets closely and find new favourites around them.

cast.name: The Poet
cast.description: The 'I' of the sonnets: older, devoted, insecure, by turns proud of his verse and ashamed of himself.

cast.name: The Young Man
cast.description: A beautiful, aristocratic young man to whom most of the first 126 sonnets are addressed.

cast.name: The Rival Poet
cast.description: Another poet who praises the young man, and whom the speaker fears in Sonnets 78–86.

cast.name: The Dark Lady
cast.description: The woman of Sonnets 127–152, whom the poet desires and distrusts.
